measure_name: Amendment 3 — Prohibit Abortion and Gender Transition Procedures for Minors Amendment (HJR 73)
description_short: YES repeals 2024's voter-approved Amendment 3 (right to reproductive freedom through fetal viability) and replaces it with a ban on abortion except in medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, with rape/incest exceptions only before 12 weeks gestation; requires parental consent for minors' abortions; also prohibits gender transition procedures (surgery/hormones) for minors.
severity_note: Direct repeal of 2024 Amendment 3 (passed 51.6%), scheduled for Nov 3 2026 general election, NOT an earlier special election (Gov. Kehoe declined to call one; it did NOT appear on the Aug 4 primary ballot). Near-total ban from conception — harsher than 2024's viability right, though it adds 12-week rape/incest exceptions the pre-2024 trigger ban lacked; bundles a gender-transition ban for minors (already state statute). Ballot language was rewritten twice by courts: Missouri Court of Appeals (Dec 2025) replaced the secretary of state's error-ridden summary to clarify a YES ends the existing right to abortion.

measure_name: Minimum Wage and Earned Paid Sick Time Amendment (Initiative Petition 2026-047, Missouri Jobs with Justice)
description_short: YES would constitutionalize a $15 minimum wage from Jan 1 2027 with automatic annual CPI increases and reinstate the earned paid sick leave mandate (1 hour per 30 worked) that the legislature's HB 567 (signed July 10 2025) repealed after voters passed Prop A in 2024. As a constitutional amendment, the legislature could not repeal it without another public vote.
severity_note: LIKELY NOT ON THE 2026 BALLOT — cleared for circulation June 24 2025 with a May 3 2026 signature deadline (~170,215 valid signatures needed), but it does not appear in May-Aug 2026 press enumerations of Missouri's nine 2026 measures and no signature submission was reported; no official failure notice located either, so marked pending rather than dead. Same substance as 2024 Prop A (passed 57.6%) but constitutional rather than statutory — a direct escalation in response to the legislature's 2025 repeal.

measure_name: Respect Missouri Voters Amendment (would be Amendment 6)
description_short: YES amends the constitution to restrict the General Assembly's ability to amend or repeal voter-approved ballot measures (requiring a supermajority ~80% legislative vote or a new public vote) and to require clear and accurate ballot summaries. Campaign formed in direct response to the legislature's 2025 repeal of Prop A's paid sick leave.
severity_note: Signatures submitted early May 2026 and campaign says it qualified, but Secretary of State Denny Hoskins REJECTED it Aug 4 2026 (multiple-subjects / self-entrenchment rationale) and tried to withdraw the ballot title his office certified a year earlier; petitioners sued in Cole County Circuit Court Aug 6 2026 to force it onto the November ballot. Litigation outcome will decide ballot placement. Novel for Missouri — no prior statewide vote on legislative-override limits; voters rejected the opposite-direction Amendment 4 (initiative restrictions) 80-20 on Aug 4 2026.

measure_name: Congressional Map Referendum (People Not Politicians veto referendum on the 2025 mid-decade redistricting law)
description_short: YES ratifies (keeps) the congressional map the legislature passed in a 2025 special session to dismantle Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City district (7-1 GOP map); NO rejects the map and restores the prior 6-2 map. The referendum suspends the map's effect if it reaches the ballot.
severity_note: More than 300,000 signatures submitted Dec 2025; local election officials verified well over the ~111,000 required, but Secretary of State Hoskins REJECTED certification Aug 4 2026, claiming redistricting laws are not subject to referendum; sponsors are suing. Constitutionally, qualified referenda must appear on the November ballot. Unprecedented in Missouri — no prior referendum on a redistricting plan; part of the national mid-decade gerrymander fight.

measure_name: Amendment 7 — 'Show-Me' Prosperity Fund Amendment
description_short: YES creates a permanent state savings/investment fund (sovereign-wealth-style) fed by appropriations and gifts, with withdrawals capped at 3% of average market value, intended eventually to generate income replacing state income, sales, and other taxes.
severity_note: Legislative referral (May 2026, sponsored by Sen. Adam Schnelting). Companion to the tax-elimination agenda whose more aggressive version (Amendment 5, income tax phaseout) was crushed 83-17 at the Aug 4 2026 primary — this is the softer, slower-burn variant.

measure_name: Amendment 8 — Election of County Sheriff Amendment (SJR 87)
description_short: YES makes county sheriff a constitutional office elected to four-year terms in most counties, recognizes sheriffs as chief law enforcement officers running jails and court security, and restricts removal of a sheriff to a quo warranto action filed only by the attorney general.
severity_note: Low-polarity legislative referral — most Missouri sheriffs are already elected; the substantive change is entrenchment plus removal protection ('constitutional sheriff' movement adjacent). No direct Missouri precedent measure.

measure_name: Amendment 1 — State Parks and Soil/Water Conservation Sales Tax Renewal
description_short: YES renewed the existing 0.1% sales/use tax for 10 years (~$140M/yr for state parks and soil and water conservation). VOTED: APPROVED Aug 4 2026 with ~82% yes.
severity_note: Routine automatic referral, renewed roughly every decade since 1984 (80% yes in 2016); non-polarizing.

measure_name: Amendment 2 — Elected Jackson County Assessor
description_short: YES requires Jackson County (Kansas City) to elect rather than appoint its county assessor, matching other charter counties. VOTED: APPROVED Aug 4 2026 with ~77% yes.
severity_note: GOP-legislature referral aimed at Jackson County's Democratic administration after the 2023 assessment controversy; county voters had already approved the change locally in Nov 2025. Low ideological extremity.

measure_name: Amendment 4 — Concurrent Congressional-District Majority for Initiated Amendments
description_short: YES would have required citizen-initiated constitutional amendments to win a majority in EACH of Missouri's eight congressional districts (not just statewide), required full initiative text availability on ballots, and banned foreign contributions. VOTED: REJECTED Aug 4 2026, ~80% no; failed in all eight districts.
severity_note: The most aggressive initiative-restriction proposal in Missouri history — under its rule, 2024 Amendment 3 (abortion), Prop A (minimum wage/sick leave), Medicaid expansion (2020), and marijuana legalization (2022) would all have failed. Decisive rejection is the direct-democracy backlash data point of the cycle.

measure_name: Amendment 5 — Income Tax Phaseout / Sales Tax Expansion
description_short: YES would have required phasing out the state individual income tax based on revenue growth and authorized expanding sales/use taxes to replace the revenue. VOTED: REJECTED Aug 4 2026, ~83% no.
severity_note: Most sweeping tax restructuring ever put to Missouri voters; landslide rejection was a major defeat for Gov. Kehoe and legislative Republicans.

measure_name: Question 6 — Right to Abortion Initiative (second required passage)
description_short: YES establishes a fundamental constitutional right to abortion until fetal viability (as determined by the treating practitioner), and afterward when needed to protect the patient's life or health. Second of two required approvals; passed 64.4% in 2024, so a 2026 YES enacts it.
severity_note: Not an expansion of practice — Nevada abortion is already legal to 24 weeks under a 1990 voter-affirmed statute; this constitutionalizes roughly the status quo (viability standard), insulating it from legislative change. Identical text to the 2024 Question 6.

measure_name: Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment (HJ 1 / SJ 247)
description_short: YES adds to the Virginia constitution 'the right to make and effectuate one's own decisions about all matters related to one's pregnancy,' protecting abortion (with post-viability regulation permitted), contraception, and pregnancy care. Passed two successive General Assemblies (2025 special session and Jan 2026), placing it on the Nov 2026 ballot.
severity_note: Virginia's first statewide abortion vote. Roughly codifies current law (legal through second trimester, ~26 weeks) rather than expanding it; strategic weight is regional — Virginia is the South's main abortion-access destination. Certified by legislative action Jan 21 2026 per Ballotpedia.

measure_name: Repeal Same-Sex Marriage Ban / Marriage Equality Amendment (HJ 9 / SJ 249)
description_short: YES repeals the dormant 2006 Marshall-Newman amendment (one-man-one-woman definition) and replaces it with a requirement that Virginia recognize marriages without regard to the sex, gender, or race of the parties.
severity_note: Goes further than the 2020 Nevada and 2024 California/Colorado/Hawaii repeals: it not only removes the defunct ban (passed 57% in 2006) but affirmatively mandates recognition — the strongest state marriage-equality text yet put to voters, positioned as an Obergefell hedge.

measure_name: Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act Initiative
description_short: YES enacts a statutory (not constitutional) right to reproductive freedom — abortion until fetal viability plus protection for contraception, fertility treatment, miscarriage care, and other pregnancy care — replacing Idaho's near-total abortion ban.
severity_note: Qualified July 13 2026 with 75,478 verified signatures across 20 of 35 legislative districts (110k+ collected, most in Idaho initiative history). Idaho's first-ever statewide abortion vote; would overturn one of the nation's strictest bans (2020 trigger law: exceptions only for life, and rape/incest reported to police). Statutory route means the legislature could later amend it — weaker durability than MO/NV/VA constitutional measures.

measure_name: HJR 4 — Legislature-Only Authority over Marijuana, Narcotics, and Psychoactive Substances Amendment
description_short: YES amends the constitution so only the legislature may legalize or change laws on marijuana, narcotics, or psychoactive substances — permanently barring citizen initiatives on drug policy (the companion medical-cannabis initiative failed to qualify in July 2026).
severity_note: Nationally novel: the first constitutional amendment anywhere to strip a subject area from the initiative process specifically to pre-empt cannabis legalization. Referred March 2025 (House 58-10, Senate 29-6) after repeated medical-marijuana petition drives.

measure_name: Question 8 — Eliminate Recreational Marijuana Sales and Allow Limited Possession Initiative
description_short: YES repeals the laws allowing licensed adult-use recreational marijuana sales and eliminates home cultivation rights, while preserving limited adult possession and leaving medical marijuana intact — dismantling the state's existing legal market.
severity_note: Certified July 9 2026 (12,551 second-round signatures verified vs 12,429 required; State Ballot Law Commission confirmed placement as Question 8). The first statewide attempt in the U.S. to repeal an operating adult-use market by initiative — directly reverses 2016 Question 4 (53.7% yes). The marquee anti-cannabis measure of 2026 after Arizona's repeal drive was dropped, Maine's missed its deadline (refiled for 2027), Florida's legalization retry fell ~96k signatures short (dead Feb 1 2026), Idaho's medical initiative failed to qualify, and Ohio's SB 56 veto referendum was suspended in March 2026.

measure_name: Adult Personal Use of Marijuana Initiative (Smart & Safe Florida) — NOT ON BALLOT
description_short: NOT ON THE 2026 BALLOT: the retry of 2024's Amendment 3 fell short — ~784,000 verified signatures vs ~880,000 required at the Feb 1 2026 deadline, after state directives invalidated ~270,000 signatures; the Florida Supreme Court declined review March 9 2026 and all signatures have expired.
severity_note: Included only to answer the cannabis-retry question definitively: dead for 2026 despite 1.4M raw signatures. 2024's version won 55.9% but missed Florida's 60% threshold. No South Dakota or North Dakota cannabis measure qualified for 2026 either.

measure_name: Constitutional Amendment I — Medicaid Expansion Conditioned on 90% Federal Funding (HJR 5001)
description_short: YES makes the state's constitutional Medicaid-expansion mandate (adopted by voters in 2022) contingent on the federal government continuing to pay at least 90% of expansion costs; if the federal match drops below 90%, the state may end or curtail expansion coverage.
severity_note: Certified March 2025 (Senate 31-3). A conditional rollback of 2022 Amendment D (56.2% yes) — softer than the outright repeal referral the SD House killed, but with real teeth given the 2025 federal reconciliation law's Medicaid cuts. Follows 2024 Amendment F (work requirements, approved). Oklahoma's parallel effort to revisit its SQ 802 Medicaid expansion failed to reach the 2026 ballot.

measure_name: State Question 832 — $15 Minimum Wage Initiative
description_short: YES would have raised the state minimum wage from $7.25 to $12 (2027), $13.50 (2028), and $15 (2029) with CPI indexing thereafter, and removed employee-classification exemptions. VOTED: REJECTED June 16 2026, ~56% no.
severity_note: Gov. Stitt scheduled the qualified initiative for a standalone low-turnout June special election rather than November — widely seen as decisive to its defeat. First red-state minimum wage initiative loss after a decade of wins (AR 2018, MO 2018/2024, NE 2022 all passed); the key 2026 labor-measure data point. No other statewide minimum wage/paid leave measure is certified for Nov 2026 nationally.

measure_name: Constitutional Amendment 1 — Direct Election of Supreme Court Justices (SCR 1611)
description_short: YES would have replaced Kansas's merit-based nominating commission with direct partisan-style elections of Supreme Court justices. VOTED: REJECTED Aug 4 2026 by a wide margin.
severity_note: This was the Kansas August 2026 measure — there was NO new direct abortion amendment; instead this was the explicit Kobach-endorsed indirect route to eventually overturn the court's 2019 Hodes abortion-rights precedent after the 2022 abortion amendment lost 59-41. Its defeat is the second statewide loss for the anti-abortion side in Kansas in four years. No other Kansas 2026 measure is certified except the November citizenship amendment.

measure_name: Citizenship Voting Requirement Amendment
description_short: YES amends Article 5 of the Kansas Constitution to state that ONLY U.S. citizens (18+, resident in their voting area) may vote in any election in the state, foreclosing any future local noncitizen voting.
severity_note: Largely symbolic (noncitizen voting is already illegal in Kansas); mirrors the wave of eight states that passed similar 'only a citizen' amendments in 2024. This is the only statewide measure on Kansas's November 2026 ballot. Illinois, for comparison, has NO statewide measures certified for 2026 as of August 2026.
